```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`g3_run_app()` starts a local Shiny app for playing, analysing and practising
the game. It needs the suggested packages shiny, bslib, htmltools and callr.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gambitR3D::g3_run_app()
# A fixed port, no browser window, and a catalogue file of your choice:
gambitR3D::g3_run_app(db_path = "~/gambitR3D/games.sqlite", port = 8080,
                      launch.browser = FALSE)
# Save native game files instead of using the catalogue:
gambitR3D::g3_run_app(db_path = FALSE)
```

The app listens on `127.0.0.1` only. Another `host` makes it reachable from
other machines without authentication, so the app warns when you choose one.
It loads nothing from the internet: the 3D library (three.js) and every icon,
script and style ship with the package, and the app sends no telemetry.

## Display is not logic

The browser only shows positions and sends intentions; every legal action
comes from the rules engine in R, and every move is checked again before it is
applied. Display settings never enter the game:

- **2D and 3D** show the same position. Switching keeps the selection and the
  position key.
- **Neutral highest / Neutral lowest** only changes how the Neutral board is
  drawn. The action ids, positions and results are identical either way.
- **Exploded view, x-ray, level isolation and the viewpoint** are display aids
  as well.

## Sections

| Section | What it does |
|---|---|
| Play | hotseat or against the search, greedy or random opponent, or a validated trained model; takeback, resignation, agreed draws (hotseat), save and load |
| Analyse | a copy of a game: ply navigation, whole-game analysis in the background, an evaluation plot, a move table and the board linked to one selected ply, tactics, a board heatmap, report download; playing from an earlier ply makes a labelled variation |
| Database | filter and page through the game catalogue, open a game in Play or Analyse, export, import with a report of duplicates and quarantined records, soft delete and restore, backup |
| Coach | a review of the live game or the analysis copy, decisions and claims with their evidence, analysed lines previewed on a copy, an explanation for any legal action |
| Training | "Practise chess": exercises with hints in order and scored attempts, a practice plan and your progress. "Train opponent": a bounded CPU training run and self-play, when the optional environment exists |
| Models | the model registry with each model's capabilities, validation checks and provenance; a validated checkpoint can be chosen as the Play opponent |
| Settings | language (English or German), light or dark theme, reduced motion, the starting board view and Neutral height, the storage folder |

The live game is never changed by Analyse, Coach or Training: they work on
copies, and every copy says so.

## The 2D boards

The seven boards are drawn as grids: the main boards B, N and W from top to
bottom (from White's side), each platform beside the board it is docked on,
with its dock and orientation written out. Overlapping coordinates on
different boards are separate squares with separate names, such as `W c3` and
`N c3`.

Select a piece to see its legal actions. Destinations are marked on the board
and also listed as buttons below it; promotions, platform moves (dock and
orientation) and castling are chosen there. Marks use shapes as well as
colour: a dot for a move, a ring for a capture, a diamond for castling.

Keyboard use: Tab moves between boards and controls, the arrow keys move
within a board, Page Up and Page Down jump between boards, Enter or Space
selects or plays, and Escape cancels. Each square has an accessible name with
its board, coordinate, piece and marks, and committed moves are announced.

## The 3D scene

The 3D scene loads on demand. Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, or choose a
viewpoint; "Reset camera" fits all seven boards in view again. A raised board
hides squares below it: when the square you point at is not the one you mean,
the app offers a chooser of the squares under the pointer, and x-ray makes the
boards see-through. Platform moves are animated, or applied at once when the
system asks for reduced motion. Without WebGL, the app stays in 2D and says
why.

## Storage

By default games are saved in a SQLite catalogue, `games.sqlite` in
`tools::R_user_dir("gambitR3D", "data")`, before a move is acknowledged. The
learner profile for practice is a JSON file in the same folder, and its
"use in a training dataset" option is off unless you switch it on. Nothing is
uploaded. Games in the native format (`.g3.json`) can be downloaded and loaded
again at any time.

## Background work

Computer moves, analyses, reviews, imports, exports and training run in
separate R processes, so the app stays responsive. Running work is listed in
the header with its progress, and can be cancelled. Work started by a session
stops when the session ends.

## Known limits

- Playing against a trained model starts a model worker for every move, which
  takes a few seconds.
- Move notation from the engine (such as `P W:c2-W:c4`) is not translated.
- There are no clocks; every game is untimed.
- The browser tests use headless Chrome on Linux. Other browsers, touch
  devices and screen readers have not been tested.
